title: 50  Scientific File Formats
text:
50.2 netCDF4
The package netCDF4 (Network Common Data Format Version 4) is installed with pip install netCDF4. netCDF4 is based on HDF5 but uses its own terminology. Access to a netCDF4 file is via the Dataset object, which corresponds to the root group. A netCDF file or the Dataset object consists of:

Groups: Groups are subdirectories of the Dataset object and can contain variables, dimensions, attributes, and further groups.
Variables: Variables correspond to datasets or NumPy arrays.
Dimensions: Dimensions describe properties of variables such as name, size, and group membership.
Attributes: Attributes describe either the entire dataset (global attributes) or individual variables. Attributes store metadata.

Dataset.description = 'Description of the dataset'
Dataset.history = 'Creation timestamp'
Dataset.source = 'Source'
Dataset.units = 'Description of measurement unit'
Dataset.calendar = 'Gregorian calendar'


These elements are structured as dictionaries and allow access via key-value pairs.

title: 50  Scientific File Formats
text:
50.3 Dataset
In this section, a NASA dataset on lightning density (number of flashes per square kilometer) is used free registration at NASA Earth required. The netCDF4 file contains various datasets (variables) obtained with satellite-based instruments. Flashes within +/- 38 degrees of the equator were measured with the Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) on the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) satellite. At higher and lower latitudes, flashes were measured with the Optical Transient Detector (OTD) on Orbview-1. The data have a resolution of 0.5 degrees. (Dataset documentation, Poetzsch 2021: 182-183)
The datasets follow the naming scheme HRFC_COM_FR

HRFC = High Resolution Full Climatology
COM = Combination of both instruments [LIS, OTD]
FR = Flash Rates [RF = Raw Flash Rates, SF = Scaled Flash Rates]


LIS/OTD 0.5 Degree High Resolution Full Climatology (HRFC) V2.3.2015 by Global Hydrometeorology Resource Center DAAC (GHRC DAAC)
DOI https://doi.org/10.5067/LIS/LIS-OTD/DATA302

title: 51  Key Takeaways (possibly as a video)
text:
Reading structured datasets may seem like an impenetrable jungle of required technical knowledge after working through this module: different technical formats, the large variety of packages and functions, and often a non-intuitive internal structure that needs to be organized. In this module, various tips were provided, which will not be repeated here individually.
The main point is that success in reading complex datasets relies less on the correct application of specific functions and more on a structured approach. Correct function usage is, of course, essential, but correct syntax can and should be looked up in the documentation (Tip 42.2).
You can achieve a structured approach with these three tips:

Work with a package that you are comfortable with and know well. This avoids errors caused by unexpected or undocumented behavior. This applies, for example, to operations with missing values or functions that fail silently.
Check key characteristics of the datasets you want to work with, such as structure, data types, value ranges, and the presence and marking of missing values. Use the available functions for descriptive data analysis (Tip 45.4). If needed, write helper functions to display certain elements or their positions.
Proceed in small steps: print the result of each intermediate step (partially) for visual inspection. Does the output make sense? Use your domain knowledge to assess it. Minor print() statements can later be removed from the script.
For very large datasets, visual inspection may not be practical. In such cases, it is helpful to create test data that reflects the expected structure of the dataset to program the steps. Then compare the results for the test data with those for the actual dataset, as described in the previous tip.

title: 53  Introduction
text:
Experimentally obtained data can be heavily affected by noise, or the relationship between the variables may be best described by a non-linear dependence. Data fitting is the process of adapting a model to a dataset in order to describe the underlying relationship between the variables, smooth the data, or estimate values between the existing data points. The goal of this process is to find a function that describes the dataset as well as possible by minimizing the deviation between the model and the actual data. This process is also referred to as modeling.
In this module, the following packages are used:

import numpy as np
import numpy.polynomial.polynomial as poly
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

The modeling of data can be generalized to the following problem:

Given are \(n\) pairs of measurement points \((x_i, y_i)\) with \(x_i, y_i \in \mathbb{R}\).
The goal is to find a model function \(y(x)\) that approximates the measurement point pairs.

One possible approach is to represent the model function as a sum of \(m\) basis functions \(\phi_i(x)\) with coefficients \(\beta_i\). \[
y(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\beta_i \cdot \phi_i(x) = \beta_1\cdot \phi_1(x) + \cdots + \beta_m\cdot \phi_m(x)
\]
The coefficients \(\beta_i\) must be determined in such a way that \(y(x)\) approximates the measurement points as well as possible – or even exactly.
As a distance measure between a model function and the measurement points, the method of least squares can be used.






Note 53.2: Method of Least Squares





Using the method of least squares, the line \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x\) is determined such that the squared distances of the predicted values \(\hat{y}\) from the actually measured values \(y\) are minimized. The values \(y_i - \hat{y_i}\) are the residuals \(e_i\). Thus, the following holds:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{N}(y_i - \hat{y_i})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} e_i = \min
\]
Graphically, the minimization of the squared distances can be illustrated as follows.

PlotCode











Regression coefficients: [ 2.93333333 -0.73333333]





x = np.arange(1, 11)
y = -x.copy() + 4
y[0] -= 2
y[2] -= 2
y[3] += 3
y[-3] += 5

lm = poly.polyfit(x, y, 1)
predicted_values = poly.polyval(x, lm)

plt.scatter(x, predicted_values, label='Predicted values', marker="^", color="tab:blue")
plt.scatter(x, y, label='Observed values', marker='o', color="tab:orange")
plt.axline(xy1=(0, lm[0]), slope=lm[1], label="Regression line", color="tab:blue")
dotted = plt.vlines(x, ymin=predicted_values, ymax=y, alpha=0.6, ls='dotted', label='Residuals')

plt.legend()
plt.show()

print("Regression coefficients:", lm)




 
The drawn straight line corresponds to the linear function \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x + e_i\). The triangular markers represent the predicted values \(\hat{y_i}\) of the linear model for the values \(x_i = \texttt{np.arange(1, 11)}\). The actual observed values \(y\) are marked with circular markers. The length of the dashed lines corresponds to the magnitude of the deviation between the observed and predicted values \(y_i - \hat{y_i}\), i.e. the residuals \(e_i\).
The goal is to find the straight line that minimizes the sum of the squared residuals. The desired values \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are the least-squares estimators.
\[
\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot \bar{x}
\]
\[
\beta_1 = { \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i- \bar{x}) \cdot (y_i - \bar{y}) \over \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 }
\]
For completeness, we derive the least-squares estimators. We are looking for values of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) such that the sum of squared residuals \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2\) is as small as possible. The sum of squared residuals is the sum of the squared differences between the observed values \(y_i\) and the values predicted by the linear function.
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 ~ = ~ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i))^2
\]
We therefore investigate a function that depends on two variables.
\[
f(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i))^2
\]
The summation symbol is shorthand notation for a sum.
\[
f(\beta_0, \beta_1) = (y_1 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1))^2 ~ + ~ (y_2 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_2))^2 ~ + ~ ... ~ (y_n - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_n))^2
\]
At the minimum of the function, both partial derivatives must be equal to zero (why this is the case is explained clearly here.)






Note 53.1: Partial derivative





A partial derivative is the derivative of a function with several variables with respect to one variable, while the other variables are treated as constants.
For a function \(f(x, y) = 2x + y^2\), the partial derivative with respect to \(x\) is written as:
\(\frac{\partial f(x, y)}{\partial x}\)

The symbol ∂ is the cursive form of the Cyrillic lowercase letter д (d) and is read as “del”. It indicates that a partial derivative is taken.
The numerator contains the function to be differentiated. The denominator contains the variable with respect to which the differentiation is performed. The expression is read as “del f of x and y with respect to del x”.

The partial derivative
\(\frac{\partial f(x, y)}{\partial x} = 2\).
The term \(y^2\) is treated as a constant (e.g. \(5^2\)) and its derivative is zero.
The partial derivative
\(\frac{\partial f(x, y)}{\partial y} = 2y\).
The term \(2x\) is treated as a constant (e.g. \(2 \cdot 3\)) and its derivative is zero.



In both partial derivatives, \(x_i\) and \(y_i\) are constants.
In the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\) is also constant;
in the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_0\) is constant accordingly.

Partial derivative with respect to the y-interceptPartial derivative with respect to the slope


For the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_0\), the chain rule applies to the outer function (top) and the inner function (middle):
\[ \begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f(\beta_0, \beta_1)}{\partial \beta_0} = 2 \cdot (y_1 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1)) ~ + ~ ... ~ (y_n - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_n)) = 2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) ~ \cdot
\newline
(0 - (1 + 0 \cdot 0)) ~ + ~ ... ~ (0 - (1 + 0 \cdot 0)) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (0 - (1 + 0 \cdot 0)) =
\newline
2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) ~ \cdot (-1)
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_0\):
\[
\frac{\partial f(\beta_0, \beta_1)}{\partial \beta_0} = -2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) = 0
\]
This expression can be simplified by dropping the prefactor \(-2\) (since \(-2 \cdot 0 = 0\)) and resolving the signs:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 \cdot x_i) = 0
\]
This can also be written as:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_0 - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_1 \cdot x_i = 0
\]
\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are constants, so
\(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_0  = \beta_0 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 = \beta_0 \cdot n\) and
\(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \beta_1 \cdot x_i = \beta_1 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} 1 \cdot x_i\).
Thus:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i - n \cdot \beta_0 - \beta_1 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = 0
\]
Dividing by \(n\), we obtain the arithmetic means
\(\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\) and
\(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\), yielding:
\[
\bar{y} - \beta_0 - \beta_1 \cdot \bar{x} = 0
\]
Rearranging gives:
\[
\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot \bar{x}
\]


For the partial derivative with respect to \(\beta_1\), the chain rule is applied again, so the outer function is differentiated in the same way:
\[ \begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial f(\beta_0, \beta_1)}{\partial \beta_1} = 2 \cdot (y_1 - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_1)) ~ + ~ ... ~ (y_n - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_n)) = 2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) ~ \cdot
\newline
(0 - (0 + 1 \cdot x_1)) ~ + ~ ... ~ (0 - (0 + 1 \cdot x_n)) ~ = ~ \sum_{i=1}^{n} -x_i =
\newline
2 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) ~ \cdot -x_i
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus:
\[
\frac{\partial f(\beta_0, \beta_1)}{\partial \beta_1} = -2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \cdot (y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot x_i)) = 0
\]
This can also be simplified by omitting the prefactor \(-2\) (since \(-2 \cdot 0 = 0\) must hold) and resolving the signs. In addition, the expression can be expanded:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}  \beta_0 \cdot x_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}  \beta_1 \cdot x_ix_i = 0
\]
Extracting constants:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - \beta_0 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i - \beta_1 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_ix_i = 0
\]
Substituting \(\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot \bar{x}\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = n \cdot \bar{x}\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - (\bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot \bar{x}) \cdot  n \cdot \bar{x} - \beta_1 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_ix_i = 0
\]
Expanding the middle term and writing \(x_i x_i\) as \(x_i^2\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot n\bar{x}\bar{x} - \beta_1 \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 = 0
\]
Combining the last two terms:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} - \beta_1 \cdot ( \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2) = 0
\]
Solving for \(\beta_1\):
\[
\beta_1 \cdot ( \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
Then: \[
\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2}
\]
Now, one can first rewrite using \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2 - n \bar{x}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2\). \[
\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]
Then—and this will be shown next—using \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\). Thus, we obtain: \[
\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]
The last step is shown starting from the result and begins with expanding the product: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i y_i - x_i \bar{y} - \bar{x} y_i + \bar{x}\bar{y})
\]
This can also be written as: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \bar{y} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x} y_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
\(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) are constants, so this can be written as \(\bar{x} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\) and \(\bar{y} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\). Since \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = n \cdot \bar{x}\) (analogously for \(y\)), we obtain:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - \bar{y} \cdot n \cdot \bar{x} - \bar{x} \cdot n \cdot \bar{y} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
Rearranging: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y} - n \bar{x}\bar{y} + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
The last term \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \bar{x}\bar{y}\) can also be written as \(n \cdot \bar{x}\bar{y}\), which yields: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y} - n \bar{x}\bar{y} + n \bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
Thus, the last two terms cancel out, leaving: \[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i - n \bar{x}\bar{y}
\]
[@Baitsch-2019, pp. 73–74]






In this chapter, the following methods for data modeling are introduced:

Polynomial interpolation

Data fitting using polynomials

Data fitting using splines

title: 54  Interpolation – Filling in the Gaps
text:
54.1 Overview
What to do when values are missing? In many datasets, there are gaps – for example, because measurements were only taken at specific points. Interpolation is a method that allows us to estimate intermediate values, i.e., values within a known range.
In contrast, extrapolation attempts to predict values outside the known range – which is generally associated with greater uncertainty.
In interpolation, we look for a model function that exactly represents the measured data.
In many practical applications, polynomials are assumed as basis functions for the model function. Advantages of polynomials:
An example of a polynomial basis:
\[ \phi_1(x)=1,\quad \phi_2(x)=x,\quad \phi_3(x)=x^2,\quad \cdots,\quad \phi_m =x^{m-1} \]

Any function can be approximated using polynomials, see Taylor series.

title: 54  Interpolation – Filling in the Gaps
text:
54.2 Polynomials
Polynomials \(P(x)\) are functions in the form of a sum of power functions with natural number exponents \((x^i, i \in \mathbb{N})\) and corresponding coefficients \(a_i\):
\[
P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i = a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0, \quad i, n \in \mathbb{N}, a_i \in \mathbb{R}
\]

The degree of a polynomial is the term with the highest exponent that has a non-zero coefficient (the so-called leading coefficient).

A polynomial of degree \(n\) has \(n\) roots, which can be complex.

In the NumPy module, polynomials are represented by their coefficients. Generally, a polynomial of degree \(n\) is represented by the following array:
[a0, a1, a2, ..., an]
For example, for \(P(x) = 3 -2x + 5x^2 + x^3\):

P = np.array([3, -2, 5, 1])
print(P)

[ 3 -2  5  1]


Functions for evaluating polynomial functions are provided by the numpy.polynomial package, specifically its module numpy.polynomial.polynomial.

import numpy.polynomial.polynomial as poly

The evaluation of a polynomial at a point or an array is done using the poly.polyval(x, c) function. This calculates the function values for the values passed in x using the function parameters c.

x = 1
y = poly.polyval(x, P)
print(f"P(x={x}) = {y}")

P(x=1) = 7.0



x = np.array([-1, 0, 1])
y = poly.polyval(x, P)
print(f"P(x={x}) = {y}")

P(x=[-1  0  1]) = [9. 3. 7.]


The Matplotlib package can be used for graphical representation in the range \(x \in [-6, 2]\).

# Generate 50 points between -6 and 2

x = np.linspace(-6, 2, 50)

# Evaluate the polynomial P at points x

y = poly.polyval(x, P)

# Plot the polynomial

plt.plot(x, y)
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y(x)')
plt.grid()

# Display the plot

plt.show()








 
To find the roots of a polynomial, the function poly.polyroots() can be used. For the polynomial above, the following roots can be determined.

roots = poly.polyroots(P)

# direct output of the array

print("Roots: ")
print(roots)

Roots: 
[-5.46628038+0.j        0.23314019-0.703182j  0.23314019+0.703182j]



print("Roots: ")

# nicer display of the array

for i, root in enumerate(roots):
    if root.imag == 0:
        print(f"  x_{i+1} = {root.real:.2}")
    else:
        print(f"  x_{i+1} = {root.real:.2} {root.imag:+.2}i")

Roots: 
  x_1 = -5.5
  x_2 = 0.23 -0.7i
  x_3 = 0.23 +0.7i


In this example, two of the roots are complex. A complex number \(z\) in Python is represented as the sum of its real part (\(Re\)) and imaginary part (\(Im\)). The latter is indicated by a trailing j, the imaginary unit.
\[
z = Re(z) + Im(z)j
\]
The roots can also be used to represent the polynomial alternatively. If \(x_i\) are the \(n\) roots, then the \(n\)-th degree polynomial is described by the following product:
\[
P(x) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left(x - x_i\right) = (x - x_1)\cdot (x - x_2) \cdot \cdots \cdot (x - x_n)
\]
For example, if 1 and 2 are the roots of a polynomial, then it is:
\[
P(x) = (x - 1)(x - 2) = 2 - 3x + x^2
\]
The function poly.polyfromroots(roots) can determine the polynomial coefficients from the roots. Based on the example above, the function call would be:

roots = [1, 2]
coefficients = poly.polyfromroots(roots)

print("Roots:", roots)
print("Coefficients:", coefficients)

Roots: [1, 2]
Coefficients: [ 2. -3.  1.]


The module numpy.polynomial.polynomial provides many convenient functions for working with polynomials. There are also functions for adding, multiplying, differentiating, or integrating polynomials. An overview can be found in the NumPy documentation.

title: 54  Interpolation – Filling in the Gaps
text:
54.3 Polynomial Interpolation
Interpolation is a method to construct data points between given measurements. A function is sought that exactly matches all measurement points, which is equivalent to the L2-norm between the function and the points being zero. For example, two points can be interpolated with a straight line.
That is, for two measurement pairs \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) with \(x_1 \neq x_2\), there exists a set of coefficients such that the L2-norm between the points and the model function
\[
y(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
\]
vanishes.

# Example data from y(x) = 2 - x

N = 50
dx = 0.25

def func(x):
    return 2 - x

x = np.array([1, 2])
y = func(x)

plt.scatter(x, y, color='C1', label="Data points", zorder=3)

x_model = np.linspace(np.min(x), np.max(x), N)
plt.plot(x_model, func(x_model), color='C0', label="Model function")

x_line = np.linspace(np.min(x)-dx, np.max(x)+dx, N)
plt.plot(x_line, func(x_line), '--', alpha=0.3, color='C0')

plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.legend()
plt.grid()

plt.show()








 
For three data points, a second-degree polynomial is used to exactly capture the points.
\[
y(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2
\]

# Example data from y(x) = -1 - 4x + 3x^2

N = 50
dx = 0.25

def func(x):
    return -1 - 4*x + 3*x**2

x = np.array([-1, 2, 3])
y = func(x)

plt.scatter(x, y, color='C1', label="Data points", zorder=3)

x_model = np.linspace(np.min(x), np.max(x), N)
plt.plot(x_model, func(x_model), color='C0', label="Model function")

x_line = np.linspace(np.min(x)-dx, np.max(x)+dx, N)
plt.plot(x_line, func(x_line), '--', alpha=0.3, color='C0')

plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.legend()
plt.grid()

plt.show()








This can be generalized: \(n\) data points can be exactly represented by a polynomial of degree (\(n-1\)). Finding the appropriate coefficients is the Lagrange interpolation problem. For the desired polynomial \(P(x)\), it holds that:
\[
P(x_i) = y_i \quad i = 1, \dots, n
\]
The existence and uniqueness of such a polynomial can be proven. The polynomial is given by:
\[  P(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i I_i(x) \] \[  \text{with}\quad I_i(x) = \prod_{j=1, i\neq j}^n \frac{x-x_j}{x_i - x_j} \]
Alternatively, a system of equations defined by a polynomial basis \(\phi_i(x)\) can be solved. For each of the \(n\) point pairs, we have:
\[  y(x_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\beta_i \cdot \phi_i(x_i) = \beta_1\cdot \phi_1(x_i) + \cdots + \beta_m\cdot \phi_m(x_i) = y_i \]
The general system of equations is
\[
\left( \begin{matrix} \phi_1(x_1) & \phi_2(x_1) & \cdots & \phi_m(x_1) \\
             \phi_1(x_2) & \phi_2(x_2) & \cdots & \phi_m(x_2) \\
             \vdots &\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
             \phi_1(x_n) & \phi_2(x_n) & \cdots & \phi_m(x_n) \\
             \end{matrix}\right).
\left(  \begin{matrix} \beta_1 \\  
      \beta_2 \\   \vdots \\   \beta_m \\
      \end{matrix} \right)
= \left(  \begin{matrix} y_1 \\  y_2 \\   \vdots \\   y_n \\ \end{matrix} \right)
\]
and using the polynomial basis
\[
\underbrace{\left( \begin{matrix} 1 & x_1 & \cdots & x_1^{n-1} \\ 1 & x_2 & \cdots & x_2^{n-1} \\ \vdots &\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n & \cdots & x_n^{n-1} \\ \end{matrix}\right)}_{V}. \left(  \begin{matrix} \beta_1 \\  \beta_2 \\   \vdots \\   \beta_m \\ \end{matrix} \right) = \left(  \begin{matrix} y_1 \\  y_2 \\   \vdots \\   y_n \\ \end{matrix} \right)
\]
The matrix \(V\) is called the Vandermonde matrix and can be solved exactly for \(m=n\) if \(x_i \neq x_j\) for all \(i, j\) with \(i\neq j\).
In Python, the interpolation problem can be solved with the function numpy.polynomial.polynomial.polyfit(), which we can call after importing the module as poly.polyfit(). The following example demonstrates its use.
The data points in the example follow the function \(f(x)\), which is only used to generate the data points:
\[ f(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{1+x^2}\]
First, we generate the data points.

def func(x):
    return 0.5 + 1/(1 + x**2)


xmin = -5
xmax = 5
x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 100)
y = func(x)


n = 5
xi = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, n)
yi = func(xi)

Now we perform the interpolation for 5 and 15 data points

P = poly.polyfit(xi, yi, n-1)
print("Interpolation coefficients:")
print(P)

Interpolation coefficients:
[ 1.50000000e+00 -5.61733355e-17 -1.71087533e-01  9.82321617e-19
  5.30503979e-03]



plt.plot(x, y, color='C0', alpha=0.5, label='generating function')
plt.plot(x, poly.polyval(x, P), color='C2', label='interpolation')
plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', label='data points', zorder=3)
plt.legend()
plt.grid()

plt.show()









n = 15
xi = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, n)
yi = func(xi)

P = poly.polyfit(xi, yi, n-1)

plt.plot(x, y, color='C0', alpha=0.5, label='generating function')
plt.plot(x, poly.polyval(x, P), color='C2', label='interpolation')
plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', label='data points', zorder=3)
plt.legend()
plt.grid()

plt.show()








 
Interpolation always satisfies the required condition \(y(x_i) = y_i\). However, high-degree polynomials often lead to unrealistic results. Large oscillations occur, which become more pronounced as the degree increases.

title: 55  Fitting
text:
Fitting involves finding a model function that does not necessarily match the measured data exactly. If a polynomial is used, its degree is much smaller than the number of data points. Linear regression is an example of fitting with a polynomial of degree one.
To fit using a polynomial, you can use the function numpy.polynomial.polynomial.polyfit(), just like with polynomial interpolation, but this time with a smaller polynomial degree.
In the following example, model data are first generated and then fitted with appropriate polynomials.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

xmin = 0
xmax = 5
x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 100)

ni = 25  # number of data points

# x-values with slight noise

xi = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, ni) + 0.2 * (2 * np.random.random(ni) - 1)

# y(x) = 2*x + 0.5 with slight noise

yi = 2 * xi + 0.5 + 2 * (2 * np.random.random(ni) - 1)

plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1')
plt.grid()
plt.show()









P1 = poly.polyfit(xi, yi, 1)

plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', zorder=3, label='Data points')
plt.plot(x, poly.polyval(x, P1), color='C0', label="Model function")
plt.grid()
plt.legend()

plt.show()








In this example, a first-degree polynomial and a second-degree polynomial are determined.

# x-values with slight noise

xi = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, ni) + 0.2*(2 * np.random.random(ni) - 1)

# y(x) = (x-2)^2 - 2x + 2.5 with slight noise

yi = (xi - 2)**2 - 2*xi + 2.5 + 2*(2 * np.random.random(ni) - 1)


P1 = poly.polyfit(xi, yi, 1)
P2 = poly.polyfit(xi, yi, 2)

plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', zorder=3, label='Data points')
plt.plot(x, poly.polyval(x, P1), color='C0', label="Model function, degree 1")
plt.plot(x, poly.polyval(x, P2), color='C2', label="Model function, degree 2")
plt.grid()
plt.legend()

plt.show()

title: 56  Splines
text:
56.1 Definition
Polynomial interpolation attempts to find a global model function. However, high-degree polynomials are generally not suitable for interpolating many points. A different approach is taken by splines, which use multiple low-degree polynomials to interpolate many points. The polynomials typically have degrees between one and three.
For \(n+1\) data points \((x_i, y_i)\), a spline function \(s_k\), here a polynomial spline, can be defined as follows:
Examples:

title: 56  Splines
text:
It is assumed that the data points are sorted, i.e., \(x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n\).
For each \(i = 0 \dots n-1\), \(s_k\) is a polynomial of degree \(k\) on the interval \(\left[x_i , x_{i+1}\right]\).
\(s_k\) is \((k-1)\)-times continuously differentiable on \(\left[x_0 , x_n \right]\).



\(k = 1\): piecewise linear spline
\(k = 3\): cubic polynomial splines (B-splines)

title: 56  Splines
text:
56.2 Cubic Splines
The cubic polynomial splines \(s_3\) (\(k = 3\)) commonly used in practice have the following properties:

\(s_3|\left[x_i,x_{i+1}\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3\)
\(s_3\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(\left[x_0,x_n\right]\), especially at the support points \(x_i\) of the data points.

The coefficients \(\beta_i\) are determined as follows:

From the \(n + 1\) data points, there are \(n\) intervals, i.e., with four coefficients each, there are a total of \(4n\) coefficients.
Exact representation of the data points (\(n + 1\) equations), i.e., \(s_3(x_i) = y_i\).
Smoothness conditions at the internal data points (\(i = 1 \dots n-1\)), each providing (\(n - 1\) equations): \[
s_3'(x_i)_- = s_3'(x_i)_+
\] \[
s_3''(x_i)_- = s_3''(x_i)_+
\] \[
s_3'''(x_i)_- = s_3'''(x_i)_+
\]
This gives \(4n - 2\) equations for \(4n\) coefficients.

To determine the two remaining equations, boundary or endpoint conditions are required. The most common conditions are:

Natural splines: the curvature at the boundary vanishes, i.e.: \[
s_3''(x_0) = s_3''(x_n) = 0
\]
Periodic splines: the slope and curvature are equal at both boundaries: \[
s_3'(x_0) = s_3'(x_n)
\] \[
s_3''(x_0) = s_3''(x_n)
\]
Hermite splines: the slopes at the boundaries are explicitly specified (here by \(u\) and \(v\)): \[
s_3'(x_0) = u
\] \[
s_3'(x_n) = v
\]

title: 56  Splines
text:
56.3 Application
The following shows two examples, \(s_1\) and \(s_3\), for creating splines in Python.

# Generate data points
n = 7
xi = np.linspace(0, np.pi, n)
yi = np.sin(xi)

For \(s_1\) splines, the function np.interp() can be used. It performs linear interpolation between given pairs of values.

# Range of values for visualizing the interpolation

x = np.linspace(0, np.pi, n*6)
y = np.sin(x)


# Interpolation
y_s1 = np.interp(x, xi, yi)


plt.plot(x, y, alpha=0.3, color='C2', lw=5,
label='Generating Function')
plt.plot(x, y_s1, color='C0', label='Interpolation')
plt.scatter(x, y_s1, s=3, zorder=3, color='C0')
plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', label='Data Points')

plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.legend();

plt.show()








 
The \(s_3\) splines can be computed using functions from the scipy module. First, the coefficients are determined (scipy.interpolate.splrep), which then allow the desired evaluation using the function scipy.interpolate.splev.

import scipy.interpolate as si


s3 = si.splrep(xi, yi)
y_s3 = si.splev(x, s3)


plt.plot(x, y, alpha=0.3, color='C2', lw=5,
label='Generating Function')
plt.plot(x, y_s3, color='C0', label='Interpolation')
plt.scatter(x, y_s3, s=3, zorder=3, color='C0')
plt.scatter(xi, yi, color='C1', label='Data Points')

plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.legend();

plt.show()

title: 57  Trend Smoothing – Reducing Noise
text:
Noisy data? A moving average smooths curves:

data = np.genfromtxt("01-daten/trenddaten-mit-rauschen.csv", delimiter=",", skip_header=1)
x = data[:, 0]
y = data[:, 1]

window = 5
weights = np.ones(window) / window
y_smooth = np.convolve(y, weights, mode='valid')

plt.plot(x, y, label="Original", alpha=0.5)
plt.plot(x[(window-1)//2:-(window//2)], y_smooth, label="Smoothed", color='red')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)
plt.title("Trend Smoothing")

plt.show()

Tip 58.1: Sample Solution: Balloon Flight





First, read in the data.

# Read data
balloon = np.genfromtxt("01-daten/messdaten-ballonfahrt.txt", delimiter=",", skip_header=1)
time = balloon[:, 0]
height = balloon[:, 1]

Next, we calculate the ascent rate \(\frac{\Delta \text{height}}{\Delta \text{time}}\). For this, we use the function np.diff(). It computes the difference of each value to its predecessor: result[i] = value[i+1] - value[i]. Therefore, no difference is calculated for the i-th value, and the result is one element shorter. The ascent rate in meters per second is obtained by dividing the two sequences.

# Calculate differences

delta_height = np.diff(height)
print("Change in height: ", delta_height[0:4])

delta_time = np.diff(time)
print("Change in time: ", delta_time[0:4])

# Calculate ascent rate

ascent_rate = delta_height / delta_time
print("Ascent rate: ", ascent_rate[0:4])

Change in height:  [ 2.18551481 -2.05482638  0.32026988  1.12796595]
Change in time:  [2.02020202 2.02020202 2.02020202 2.02020202]
Ascent rate:  [ 1.08182983 -1.01713906  0.15853359  0.55834314]


Using numpy.polynomial.polynomial.polyfit(), we first fit a third-degree polynomial, then use numpy.polynomial.polynomial.polyval() to evaluate the fitted data.

poly3_ascent_rate = poly.polyfit(time[:-1], ascent_rate, deg = 3)

fit_ascent_rate = poly.polyval(x = time[:-1], c = poly3_ascent_rate)


# plotting

plt.suptitle("Balloon Flight")

## subplot: altitude over time

plt.subplot(1, 3, 1)
plt.scatter(time, altitude)
plt.title("Altitude")
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Altitude (m)")
plt.grid(True)

## subplot: ascent rate over time

## length of the ascent_rate array is n-1

plt.subplot(1, 3, 2)
plt.scatter(time[:-1], ascent_rate)
plt.title("Ascent Rate")
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Ascent Rate (m/s)")
plt.grid(True)

## subplot: cubic polynomial fitted ascent rate over time

## length of the ascent_rate array is n-1

plt.subplot(1, 3, 3)
plt.plot(time[:-1], fit_ascent_rate)
plt.title("Fitted\nAscent Rate")
plt.xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.ylabel("Ascent Rate (m/s)")
plt.grid(True)

58.3 Exercise: Neutron Scattering
The file ‘01-daten/neutronen.txt’ contains data from a neutron scattering experiment. The file header:

# Read file header as a string
neutrons = np.genfromtxt("01-daten/neutronen.txt", delimiter="\t", max_rows=4, dtype='str')
print(neutrons)

[['E(MeV)' 'sigma(mb)' 'Delta sigma(mb)']

In the column ‘E(MeV)’, the energy of a neutron fired at a target is listed in mega-electronvolts. In the column ‘sigma(mb)’, the cross section, measured in millibarns (mb), is listed. In the column ‘Delta sigma(mb)’, the uncertainty of the measured cross section, also in millibarns (mb), is listed.

Read in the data
Try to fit the first two columns with a polynomial of a suitable degree and display the result graphically.
Fit the data again, but this time use splines.
Display the result graphically as well and compare it with the polynomial fit.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of each method?







Tip 58.3: Sample Solution: Neutron Scattering






Read in the data


neutrons = np.genfromtxt("01-daten/neutronen.txt", delimiter="\t", skip_header=1)
neutron_energy = neutrons[:, 0]
cross_section = neutrons[:, 1]

plt.plot(neutron_energy, cross_section, label="Measured data", alpha=0.5)
plt.xlabel("Neutron Energy (MeV)")
plt.ylabel("Cross Section (mb)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.show()








 



Polynomial and Spline Fitting




# Polynomial

polynomial5 = poly.polyfit(neutron_energy, cross_section, deg=5)
fit = poly.polyval(x=neutron_energy, c=polynomial5)

# Splines with SciPy

spline3 = si.splrep(neutron_energy, cross_section)
y_spline3 = si.splev(neutron_energy, spline3)

# Splines with NumPy

x_new = np.linspace(neutron_energy.min(), neutron_energy.max(), num=50)
y_spline1 = np.interp(x_new, neutron_energy, cross_section)  # linear interpolation


Graphical Representation


plt.figure(figsize=[7, 5])

# Comparison with cubic splines

plt.subplot(2, 1, 1)
plt.plot(neutron_energy, cross_section, linewidth=5, alpha=0.3, label="Measurement data")
plt.plot(neutron_energy, fit, label="Fitted polynomial")
plt.plot(neutron_energy, y_spline3, linestyle='dashdot', label="Cubic splines")
plt.xlabel("Neutron energy (MeV)")
plt.ylabel("Cross section (mb)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

# Comparison with linear splines

plt.subplot(2, 1, 2)
plt.plot(neutron_energy, cross_section, linewidth=5, alpha=0.3, label="Measurement data")
plt.plot(neutron_energy, fit, label="Fitted polynomial")
plt.plot(x_new, y_spline1, linestyle='dotted', label="Linear splines")
plt.xlabel("Neutron energy (MeV)")
plt.ylabel("Cross section (mb)")
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








 
5.: The splines match the data exactly. This can be an advantage if no smoothing of the data is desired. The polynomial, on the other hand, is not fitted exactly to the data. However, all data points can be approximated using a single model equation.

title: 59  The Principle of Measurements
text:
59.1 Measurement
In this module, the following packages are used:
Physical quantities are determined with the help of measuring instruments. These assign a numerical value to the actual characteristic relative to a reference system.
An example: “Johanna measures 173 centimeters on the measuring board.”
Measured values can only ever be approximations of the true value of the underlying physical quantity for various reasons. On the one hand, a person’s height varies over the course of the day. On the other hand, the measurement result also depends on the scale used. If the measurement had been taken in the imperial system, Johanna’s height would have been determined as 68 inches, which corresponds to 172.72 centimeters.
The measurement result is therefore not an exact representation of the actual characteristic. A well-known example of the uncertainty associated with the measurement process is the coastline paradox: The result of measuring irregular coastlines becomes larger the smaller the chosen measurement segments are.

title: 59  The Principle of Measurements
text:
Important 59.1: Measurement



“A measurement is the experimental process by which a specific value of a physical quantity is determined as a multiple of a unit or reference value.
The measurement first yields a measured value. However, due to external influences, this value practically never agrees exactly with the true value of the measured quantity but shows some measurement deviation. A complete measurement result is obtained when the measured value is supplemented with quantitative statements about the expected magnitude of the measurement deviation. In metrology, this is regarded as part of the measurement task and thus part of the measurement itself.”
Measurement, by various authors, is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 and available on Wikipedia. 2025

An ideal measurement is a direct measurement or the desired value depends linearly on the measured value.
An ideal measurement is accurate and precise.




59.1.1 Direct and indirect measurement
In a direct measurement, the measured quantity is obtained by direct comparison with a standard or a defined reference system.









Beam balance







Folding rulers






Figure 59.2: Direct measurement



Folding rulers by Fst76 are licensed under CC-BY-SA 3.0 and available on Wikimedia. 2014

 
In an indirect measurement, the measured quantity is related to another physical quantity.









Spring scale







Laser distance measurement






Figure 59.3: Indirect measurement



Spring scale by Amada44 is licensed under CC-BY-SA-3.0 unported and available on Wikimedia. 2016
Observe the Moon was published by NASA and is available at nasa.gov. 2010

 


59.1.2 Accuracy and precision








Accuracy







Precision






The accuracy of a measurement describes how close the measured values are to the real value. Accuracy can only be determined when accepted reference values exist.


The precision of a measurement describes how well the individual measured values agree with each other. The precision of a measurement is determined using the standard deviation of the sample.




Figure 59.4: Accuracy and precision

title: 59  The Principle of Measurements
text:
59.2 Measurement series
To reduce measurement uncertainty, a measured value can be repeatedly recorded as part of a measurement series. The best estimate of the measured quantity is given by the arithmetic mean.
The arithmetic mean of a measurement series \(\bar{x}\) is the sum of all individual measured values \(x_i\) divided by the number of measurements \(N\).
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i
\]
Using the arithmetic mean, we can assess the scatter of measured values and the precision of the measurement by calculating the variance and standard deviation.

VarianceStandard deviation


Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean.
\[
\text{Var}(x_i) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2
\]


The square root of the variance is the standard deviation. It has the same unit as the measured values and is therefore easier to interpret. The standard deviation \(s\) is calculated as:
\[
s_{N} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]
For samples, the sample variance is used. The following applies to the standard deviation of a sample:
\[
s_{N-1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]



Since the variance is the square of the standard deviation \(s\), it is often denoted as \(s^{2}\).






Warning 59.1: Standard deviation and variance in the population



In statistics, formulas are often written with Greek letters when referring to the entire population.
The population mean is also called the expected value and is denoted by the Greek letter \(\mu\) (mu). The standard deviation of the expected value is denoted by \(\sigma\) (sigma).
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \mu)^2}
\]


Using the standard deviation, the standard error of the mean can be determined. The standard error of the mean indicates how closely the arithmetic mean of the sample approximates the population mean (more on this shortly) and is also called the sampling error. It is calculated from the standard deviation and the square root of the sample size.
\[
\sigma_{\bar{x}} ~ = ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{N}}
\]
Since the population standard deviation is usually unknown, the standard error of the mean is estimated using the sample standard deviation.
\[
\sigma_{\bar{x}}~ = ~ \frac{s_{n-1}}{\sqrt{N}}
\]
Sometimes, the standard error is rewritten in long form:
\[
\sigma_{\bar{x}} ~ = ~ \frac{s_{n-1}}{\sqrt{N}} ~ = ~ \sqrt{\frac{1}{N(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^{N}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]
The standard error becomes smaller (the measurement becomes more precise) the smaller the population variance and the larger the sample size.
This can be illustrated using a simulated dice experiment. For an ideal, fair die, each face appears equally often. The expected value of a six-sided die is:
\[
\frac{1}{6} \sum_{i=1}^{i=6}(x_i) ~ = ~ 3.5
\]
The standard deviation of a fair six-sided die is:
\[
\sqrt{\frac{1}{6} \sum_{i=1}^{i=6}(x_i - 3.5)^2} ~ \approx ~ 1.71
\]
Since the population variance is known, the standard error of the mean depends only on the sample size.

59.2.1 Experiment: Distribution characteristics
In a simulated experiment, 100 people each roll a die 3, 10, and 50 times and compute the mean of their rolls. Because a fair die is simulated, the standard error can be calculated using the population standard deviation.

Resultsgraphical representationCode




Rolls per person: 3             Sample size: 300
Smallest mean: 1.00     Largest mean: 6.00
Sample mean: 3.57       Standard error: 0.10

Rolls per person: 10            Sample size: 1000

Sample mean: 3.49       Standard error: 0.05

Rolls per person: 50            Sample size: 5000
Smallest mean: 2.98     Largest mean: 4.36
Sample mean: 3.50       Standard error: 0.02



As the number of rolls increases, the minimum and maximum of the individual average values as well as the sample mean approach the expected value.
Note: Since the script is generated dynamically, the random numbers were created using a fixed seed value.


The frequency of the individual mean values is shown in the following histograms.











Calculation

people = 100
population_std_dev = np.arange(1, 7).std(ddof = 0)
seed = 1

# 3 rolls
rolls = 3

## People are in rows (axis = 0), rolls in columns (axis = 1)
dice3 = np.random.default_rng(seed = seed).integers(low = 1, high = 6, endpoint = True, size = (people, rolls)) # high is exclusive if endpoint = False

## Compute row-wise mean with np.array.mean(axis = 1)
print(f"Rolls per person: {rolls}\t\t\t\t",
      f"Sample size: {rolls * people}\n",
      f"Smallest mean: {dice3.mean(axis = 1).min():.2f}\t\t",
      f"Largest mean: {dice3.mean(axis = 1).max():.2f}\n",
      f"Sample mean: {dice3.mean():.2f}\t\t",
      f"Standard error: {population_std_dev / ( dice3.size ** (1/2) ):.2f}\n",
      sep = "")

# 10 rolls
rolls = 10

## People are in rows (axis = 0), rolls in columns (axis = 1)
dice10 = np.random.default_rng(seed = seed).integers(low = 1, high = 6, endpoint = True, size = (people, rolls)) # high is exclusive if endpoint = False

## Compute row-wise mean with np.array.mean(axis = 1)
print(f"Rolls per person: {rolls}\t\t\t",
      f"Sample size: {rolls * people}\n",
      f"Smallest mean: {dice10.mean(axis = 1).min():.2f}\t\t",
      f"Largest mean: {dice10.mean(axis = 1).max():.2f}\n",
      f"Sample mean: {dice10.mean():.2f}\t\t",
      f"Standard error: {population_std_dev / ( dice10.size ** (1/2) ):.2f}\n",
      sep = "")

# 50 rolls
rolls = 50

## People are in rows (axis = 0), rolls in columns (axis = 1)
dice50 = np.random.default_rng(seed = seed).integers(low = 1, high = 6, endpoint = True, size = (people, rolls)) # high is exclusive if endpoint = False

## Compute row-wise mean with np.array.mean(axis = 1)
print(f"Rolls per person: {rolls}\t\t\t",

Sample variance: 58.51

Tip 59.1: Sample Solution: Distribution Statistics






def distribution_statistics(x, output = True):

  # Determine the number of measurements
  N = len(x)

  # Calculate the arithmetic mean
  sample_mean = sum(x) / N

  # Calculate the sample variance
  sample_variance = sum((x - sample_mean) ** 2) / (N - 1)

  # Calculate the sample standard deviation
  sample_std_dev = sample_variance ** (1/2)

  # Calculate the sampling error
  sampling_error = sample_std_dev / (N ** (1/2))

  # Output
  if output: # output = True
    print(f"N: {N}\n",
          f"Arithmetic mean: {sample_mean:.2f}\n",
          f"Sampling error: {sampling_error:.2f}\n",
          f"Sample variance: {sample_variance:.2f}\n",
          f"Sample standard deviation: {sample_std_dev:.2f}",
          sep = '')

  else: # output = False
    return N, sample_mean, sampling_error, sample_variance, sample_std_dev

distribution_statistics(guinea_pigs['len'])






59.2.3 Variance and Standard Deviation with NumPy and Pandas
The NumPy and Pandas modules have built-in functions for calculating variance and standard deviation. Variance and standard deviation are calculated using the functions np.var() and np.std(), or the methods pd.var() and pd.std(). The parameter ddof (delta degrees of freedom) controls which denominator is used for calculating variance in the form N - ddof. While NumPy’s default is ddof=0, Pandas calculates the sample variance with the default value ddof=1.

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
60.1 Adjusting a Normal Distribution
As the sample size increases, the estimate of the expected value becomes more accurate. Mathematically, this observation is explained by the central limit theorem. For example, when rolling multiple dice, outcomes far from the expected value become increasingly unlikely. This can already be demonstrated with just a few dice (see example).
The convergence of measurements toward a population mean as the sample size increases also holds when the population mean and variance are unknown. As the sample size grows, the measurements approach the normal distribution, which is also known as the Gaussian bell curve after its discoverer, Carl Friedrich Gauss.
The convergence of the distribution of measurements to the normal distribution for larger samples can be illustrated using the body mass of penguins from the palmerpenguins dataset.
The dataset contains data for three penguin species.
Among other things, body weight was measured in grams, which is recorded in the column body_mass_g. The weight distribution of the three species is displayed using a histogram for each species. Additionally, the sample mean and sample standard deviation are calculated for each species. These values can be used to compute a normal distribution curve and overlay it on the histogram (as shown in Note 60.3). This allows a visual check of whether the empirical distribution of the sample values corresponds to a normal distribution with the same mean and standard deviation. (For measurement data, this is often less clear than for the distribution of dice rolls.)
The normal distribution is a density curve that a histogram approaches as the number of measurements goes to infinity and the class width approaches zero.
To approximate the distribution of a dataset with a normal distribution, its mean and standard deviation are inserted into the normal distribution’s function. In Python, these calculations can be performed directly. More convenient are the functions provided by the SciPy package, which will be presented in detail in the next section. The following example shows calculation and visualization using Python and SciPy.

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
Note 60.3: Calculating and plotting density curves





Let’s consider the distribution statistics of the group of guinea pigs that received a dose of 2 milligrams of vitamin C.

print(distribution_characteristics(dose2), "\n");

dose2_mean = distribution_characteristics(dose2, output = False)[1]
dose2_std = distribution_characteristics(dose2, output = False)[4]

print("Exact mean:", dose2_mean)
print("Exact standard deviation:", dose2_std)

N: 20
Arithmetic mean: 26.10
Sample error: 0.84
Sample variance: 14.24
Sample standard deviation: 3.77
None 

Exact mean: 26.1
Exact standard deviation: 3.7741503052098744


If we insert the standard deviation and the arithmetic mean into the normal distribution function, we get:
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{3.7742 \sqrt{2\pi}} ~ e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-26.10}{3.7742}\right)^2}
\]
\[
f(x) = 0.1057 \cdot e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-26.10}{3.7742}\right)^2}
\]
In Python, these calculations can be implemented and visualized:

# Plot histogram of probability density

plt.hist(dose2, bins=7, density=True, edgecolor='black', alpha=0.6)
plt.title('Length of tooth-forming cells in guinea pigs')

# Axis labels

plt.xlabel('Length of tooth-forming cells (μm)')
plt.ylabel('Probability density')

# Calculate normal distribution

hist, bin_edges = np.histogram(dose2, bins=7)

x_values = np.linspace(min(bin_edges), max(bin_edges), 100)

## Compute normal distribution function in Python

y_values = 1 / (dose2_std * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) * np.exp(- (x_values - dose2_mean) ** 2 / (2 * dose2_std ** 2))
plt.plot(x_values, y_values, label='Normal Distribution', lw=4)

## Using SciPy

y_values_scipy = scipy.stats.norm.pdf(x_values, loc=dose2_mean, scale=dose2_std)
plt.plot(x_values, y_values_scipy, label='SciPy', linestyle='dashed')

plt.legend()
plt.show()








The distribution of the length of tooth-forming cells in guinea pigs that received a dose of 2 milligrams of vitamin C could follow a normal distribution. However, due to the small sample size, this is difficult to assess.

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
60.2 The SciPy Package
Functions for calculating density curves can be imported via the SciPy package. The stats module (statistical functions) includes numerous functions for hypothesis testing. Functions for the normal distribution are called as follows:

import scipy
print("Probability density of the normal distribution at x = 0:", scipy.stats.norm.pdf(0), "\n")

Probability density of the normal distribution at x = 0: 0.3989422804014327 



For the normal distribution, four functions are relevant:












Description The function scipy.stats.norm.pdf(x) calculates the density of the normal distribution at the point x (pdf = probability density function). x can also be an array — the curve on the left was calculated using the command scipy.stats.norm.pdf(np.linspace(-4, 4, 100)).













Description
The function scipy.stats.norm.cdf(x) calculates the proportion of values to the left of x (cdf = cumulative density function).













Description
The function scipy.stats.norm.ppf(q) is the quantile function of the normal distribution and the inverse of the cumulative density function (cdf). The function computes, for \(0 \le q \le 1\), the value x to the left of which the proportion q of all values lies and to the right of which the proportion 1-q lies (ppf = percentile point function).













Description
The function scipy.stats.norm.rvs(size) draws size random numbers from the normal distribution.
Note: The random numbers are generated dynamically in the script.



The shape of the normal distribution can be adjusted using the parameters loc = mean and scale = standard_deviation. By default, the standard normal distribution with loc = 0 and scale = 1 is used. The function parameters can be single values (scalars) or arrays/lists.

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
60.4 Confidence Intervals
Inferential statistics is based on the principle of drawing conclusions about the true population value from sample values. The reasoning is as follows:

When a sample is drawn from a population, the sample values are normally distributed around the population mean. For a normal distribution:

68.27% of all values lie within \(\pm 1 ~ s\),
95.45% of all values lie within \(\pm 2 ~ s\), and
99.73% of all values lie within \(\pm 3 ~ s\).

With the same probability distribution, the unknown population mean is distributed around a random value from the sample.
The expected value can be estimated with a certain probability using the standard error of the mean of a sample. A confidence level is chosen, i.e., the probability that the expected value actually lies within the estimated range. The opposite case, where the expected value does not lie within the estimated range, is called the significance or alpha level, denoted by the Greek letter \(\alpha\). \(\alpha\) ranges from 0 to 1, and the confidence level is \(1 - \alpha\) (see: Type I and II errors).

the expected value lies in 68.27% of cases within \(\pm 1 ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\),
the expected value lies in 95.45% of cases within \(\pm 2 ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\), and
the expected value lies in 99.73% of cases within \(\pm 3 ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\).


Often, the alpha level \(\alpha = 0.05\) or a 95% confidence interval is chosen, which corresponds to \(\pm 1.96 ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\). This, however, applies only to large samples. For small sample sizes, sample means follow the t-distribution, which will be introduced in the next section.
to do Maik: here one could / should introduce one-sided and two-sided hypothesis tests and the concept of “alpha-half”. This could also be illustrated nicely with arrows going only to the right or both sides.
The following example visually demonstrates the idea that with a certain probability, one can infer the population mean (expected value) from the sample mean.






NotePrinciple of Inferential Statistics






Standard Normal DistributionSingle MeasurementSample N = 12Code


In a normal distribution, values near the expected value occur more frequently than values far from it. How often or rarely a value occurs relative to the mean can be expressed using the standard deviation.
The chart below shows randomly drawn values and a normal distribution curve.











A single measurement from the distribution almost never equals the expected value. However, one knows that values close to the expected value occur more frequently than those far away.











The mean of a sample almost never equals the expected value. However, the expected spread, expressed in units of the standard error of the mean, is significantly narrower than that of a single observation. This is also clearly visible in the graph. The density curve is much narrower and taller than the normal distribution curve of a single measurement. This is due to the small standard deviation in the sample of ~0.2, which compresses the curve.











Code for the panel Sample N = 12

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy

# Parameters of the standard normal distribution
mu, sigma = 0, 1  # mean and standard deviation

# Generate data
seed = 4
np.random.seed(seed = seed)
data = np.random.default_rng().normal(mu, sigma, 1000)

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize = (8.5, 6))

# Plot histogram
array, bins, patches = plt.hist(data, bins = 30, density = True, alpha = 0.6, color = 'lightgoldenrodyellow', edgecolor='black')

# Draw mean line
mean_line = plt.axvline(mu, color = 'steelblue', linestyle = 'solid', linewidth = 3)

# Draw positive and negative standard deviations
pos_std_lines = [plt.axvline(mu + i * sigma, color = 'steelblue', linestyle = 'dotted', linewidth = 2) for i in range(1, 4)]
neg_std_lines = [plt.axvline(mu - i * sigma, color = 'steelblue', linestyle = 'dotted', linewidth = 2) for i in range(1, 4)]

# Normal distribution curve
x_values = np.linspace(min(bins), max(bins), 100)
y_values = 1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) * np.exp(- (x_values - mu) ** 2 / (2 * sigma ** 2))
normal_dist_curve = plt.plot(x_values, y_values, color = 'steelblue', linestyle = 'solid', linewidth = 2)

# Sample
N = 12
np.random.seed(seed = 4)
sample = np.random.default_rng().normal(mu, sigma, N)

sample_std = sample.std(ddof = 1)
sample_mean = sample.mean()
standard_error =  sample_std / np.sqrt(len(sample))

# Histogram calculation for sample
# hist, bins = np.histogram(sample, bins = 30, density = True)

# Standard error curve for sample
# x_values = np.linspace(min(bins), max(bins), 100)
x = np.linspace(sample_mean - 4 * sample_std, sample_mean + 4 * sample_std, 100)
y_values = scipy.stats.t.pdf(x = x_values, df = N - 1, loc = sample_mean, scale = standard_error) # t-distribution

# Draw sample mean
mean_sample = plt.axvline(sample_mean, color = 'black', linestyle = 'solid', linewidth = 2)

# Draw sample distribution curve
sample_dist_curve = plt.plot(x_values, y_values, color = 'black', linestyle = 'solid', linewidth = 2)

# Legend
plt.legend([normal_dist_curve[0], mean_line, neg_std_lines[0], mean_sample, sample_dist_curve[0]],
           ['Standard normal distribution', 'Mean', 'Standard deviation', 'Sample mean', 't-distribution'],
           loc='upper right', handlelength = 3)

plt.title('Standard Normal Distribution')
plt.xlabel('Standard deviation')
plt.ylabel('Probability density')

plt.show()

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
60.5 The t-Distribution
The t-distribution was discovered by William Sealy Gosset (though not the very first) and popularized. It is also known as Student’s t-distribution: Since Gosset’s employer, the Guinness Brewery, did not allow him to publish the discovery, Gosset published under the pseudonym Student. (Wikipedia)
The t-distribution describes the distribution of sample means with unknown population variance, where the standard error is estimated using the sample standard deviation. Compared to the normal distribution, the t-distribution has the degrees of freedom as an additional parameter.






Important 60.2: Degrees of Freedom





“The number of independent pieces of information that go into estimating a parameter is called the degrees of freedom. In general, the degrees of freedom of an estimate of a parameter equal the number of independent individual pieces of information used in the estimate minus the number of parameters that are estimated as intermediate steps in calculating the parameter itself. For example, \(n\) values are used to compute the sample variance. Nevertheless, the degrees of freedom are \(n - 1\), because the mean is estimated as an intermediate step, losing one degree of freedom.”
Degrees of freedom (statistics), by various authors, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, retrieved from Wikipedia. 2025



The general probability density function of the t-distribution is:
\[
f(x) = \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu + 1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\nu \pi} , \Gamma\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu + 1}{2}}
\]

\(\nu\) (nu) is the degrees of freedom.
\(\Gamma\) is the Gamma function, which for integer arguments \(n\) satisfies \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\).

Since the degrees of freedom for calculating the sample mean is \(n - 1\), it can also be written as: \[
f(x) = \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{(n-1) \pi} , \Gamma\left(\frac{n-1}{2}\right)} \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{n-1}\right)^{-\frac{n}{2}}
\]

\(n\) is the sample size.

The scipy.stats module provides functions to compute the t-distribution:

scipy.stats.t.pdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1) computes the probability density for values x for a t-distribution with df degrees of freedom, mean loc, and standard deviation scale (pdf = probability density function).
scipy.stats.t.cdf(x, df, loc=0, scale=1) computes the cumulative probability left of x (cdf = cumulative density function).
scipy.stats.t.ppf(q, df, loc=0, scale=1) is the quantile function of the t-distribution (ppf = percentile point function).
scipy.stats.t.rvs(df, loc=0, scale=1, size=1) generates size random samples from the t-distribution.

Function parameters can be single values (scalars) or arrays/lists.
As the sample size increases, the t-distribution approaches the normal distribution. A common rule of thumb is \(n > 30\). The graphic below shows the convergence of the t-distribution to the normal distribution.

PlotCode














x_values = np.linspace(-4, 4, 100)

# Normal distribution

y_values = scipy.stats.norm.pdf(x_values)
plt.plot(x_values, y_values, color='black', lw=3, label='Normal distribution')

# plt.ylim(bottom=0, top=0.5)

# t-distributions

marker = [".", "1", "x"]

[plt.plot(x_values, scipy.stats.t.pdf(x_values, df=(i + (i - 1) * 2)), linestyle='dotted', marker=marker[i - 1], linewidth=2, alpha=0.6, label='df = ' + str((i + (i - 1) * 2))) for i in range(1, 4)]

plt.suptitle('The df Parameter of the t-Distribution')
plt.xlabel('Standard deviation')
plt.ylabel('Probability density')
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.show()




The maximum of the t-distribution is less dense, but the tails of the distribution are denser than those of the normal distribution.
Thus, for the t-distribution of sample means, we have:
\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{n-1} \cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]

\(t\) is the return value of the function scipy.stats.t.ppf(q, df = n - 1, loc = 0, scale = 1)
q is the chosen alpha level, or for a two-sided hypothesis test \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) and \(1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}\).
The result is the return value of the functions:

scipy.stats.t.ppf(q = alpha/2, df = n - 1, loc = sample_mean, scale = sample_standard_error)
scipy.stats.t.ppf(q = 1 - alpha/2, df = n - 1, loc = sample_mean, scale = sample_standard_error)








Tip 60.1: t-distribution or normal distribution?





On a computer, the t-distribution is just as easy (or difficult) to compute as the normal distribution. Since the t-distribution approaches the normal distribution for larger sample sizes anyway, it is recommended to always use the t-distribution.

title: 60  The Normal Distribution
text:
60.6 Exercise: Confidence Intervals

Estimate the body weight of female penguins of the species Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo observed in the year 2008.
Which confidence interval can you report for the mean values if a confidence level of 90% is required?







Tip 60.2: Tip and Sample Solution





The following steps will help you solve the task:

Determine the sample mean \(\bar{x}\).
Determine the sample standard deviation \(s\), the sample size \(N\), and the standard error \(\frac{s}{\sqrt{N}}\).
Determine the z- or t-values from the normal or t-distribution for the chosen confidence level — for a two-sided hypothesis test use \(\frac{\alpha}{2}\) and \(1 - \frac{\alpha}{2}\).
Compute the confidence interval \(\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha / 2} ~ \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\).







TipSample Solution





Define alpha level and select penguins

alpha = 1 - 0.9
data = penguins[(penguins['sex'] == sex) & (penguins['year'] == year)]


Determine sample means.


penguin_means = data['body_mass_g'].groupby(by=data['species']).mean()
print(penguin_means)

penguin_sizes = data['body_mass_g'].groupby(by = data['species']).size()
penguin_stderrors = penguin_stds / np.sqrt(penguin_sizes)

title: 61  Linear Parameter Estimation
text:
61.1 Measurement Series: Hooke’s Law
Many physical quantities are measured indirectly. Frequently, there is a linear relationship between the measured quantity and the desired quantity. In practice, the data of a measurement series are never exact and are affected by more or less significant deviations from the true value of the desired quantity. Linear parameter estimation is a method used to determine, from a set of data, the value that minimizes the deviations of individual measured values.
Possible sources:
Hooke’s law, named after the English scientist Robert Hooke, describes the relationship between the force \(F\) and the change in length \(\Delta x\) of a spring by the equation
\(F = k \cdot \Delta x\),
where \(k\) is the spring constant.
The spring constant is a fundamental property of elastic materials and indicates how much force is required to stretch or compress a spring by a certain length. Hooke’s law states that the deformation of an elastic body is proportional to the applied force, as long as the spring is not stretched or compressed beyond its elastic range.
In an experiment, Hooke’s law was tested. A metal spring hanging from a mount has a (variable) weight attached. Below it, at some distance, an ultrasonic sensor is placed for distance measurement. The distance between the underside of the weight attached to the spring and the ultrasonic sensor is the measured distance.
The weights were determined with an accuracy of \(\epsilon_{m} = 0.5\ \mathrm{g}\) using a kitchen scale.
The measurement series is provided as a CSV file located at the path 01-daten/hooke_data.csv. The file is read using Pandas.
file_path = "01-daten/hooke_data.csv"
hooke = pd.read_csv(filepath_or_buffer=file_path, sep=';')

Important 61.1: Outlier





In statistics, a measurement is called an outlier if it deviates strongly from the rest of the data series. Multiple outliers can occur in a dataset. These values can be removed from the dataset to improve estimation if it is assumed that they are caused by measurement errors or other disturbances.
One way to identify outliers is the z-transformation. A threshold must be chosen, above which a measurement is classified as an outlier, e.g., 2.5 or 3 standard deviations. A variety of outlier tests have been developed in statistics (see Outlier tests).
However, classifying a measurement as an outlier cannot be based solely on statistical methods; it is always a judgment decision based on your domain knowledge. Not all extreme values are automatically invalid—they can occur with a certain statistical probability (see chapter on the Normal distribution). Such values are referred to as valid extreme values.
